newsitem.title: USA: U.S. steps up verbal fight with EU over wheat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. steps up verbal fight with EU over wheat.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman stepped up a verbal battle over the world wheat market on Friday, issuing a new warning to the European Union that he will fight subsidies with subsidies.
He said the U.S. administration was watching closely to see if EU wheat pricing becomes aggressive and threatened to restart U.S. subsidies if it does.
"If, in fact, we see a serious and appreciable interest by the Europeans to weave their subsidized tentacles throughout the world, then we will take action," he said.
World grain markets have been largely free of export subsidies for more than a year, because high prices and dwindling supplies made them unnecessary.
But the European Union restarted wheat subsidies last week, with officials there saying they were necessary to bridge a temporary gap between world and EU prices.

Glickman said at a news briefing that although there was no contingency plan on paper yet, his officials were already talking to other U.S. agencies about using the Export Enhancement Program (EEP) of subsidies.
The program is funded at $100 million for fiscal 1997, which starts next week, half the level for 1996, and Glickman said he would ask Congress for more funds if necessary.
"If the subsidies are enhanced overseas, and if we think that the threat is great to United States grain production, we'll ask Congress for additional money," he said.

Despite the strong talk, U.S. analysts said subsidies were unlikely in the short term, pointing to a government report due on Monday that is expected to say wheat stocks on Sept. 1 were at their lowest levels in two decades.

The European Commission's director general for agriculture, Guy Legras, sought on Wednesday to calm U.S. fears, saying the EU was planning no measures to boost wheat exports and wanted no confrontation with the United States.

But Pat Roberts, who chairs the powerful Agriculture Committee in the House of Representatives and who is from a major wheat-growing district in Kansas, said on Wednesday Glickman should think hard about using the EEP.
"The pressure is building within the wheat industry towards reactivation of EEP," Carl Schwensen of the National Association of Wheat Growers said.
Schwensen said he would also like to see Glickman take a stand against Australia's and Canada's pricing policies.
A group representing wheat growers in North Dakota wrote to Glickman on Thursday asking him to renew the subsidies.
A report on Thursday by the International Grains Council (IGC) gave a gloomy outlook for wheat prices, which would make a subsidy war more likely.
